body: The seven-story Bronze Palace in Anuradhapura, also known as the Lowamahapaya, is an awe-inspiring architectural wonder that radiates grandeur and luxury. Currently, visitors can only view the foundation and the ground floor granite pillars, which are symmetrically aligned. The sheer size of these remnants reveals the intricate design of this historic structure, showcasing the advanced engineering skills of ancient Sri Lankan craftsmen.Standing before this magnificent palace, one cannot help but feel a rush of excitement and wonder at the rich history and cultural significance it embodies. Each level of the palace would have been adorned with elaborate carvings and sculptures, providing a unique glimpse into the past and leaving visitors in awe of the ingenuity and creativity of those who constructed it centuries ago.As you explore the area, you may be delighted to encounter many monkeys and rare black-necked herons, adding to the enchanting atmosphere of this remarkable site.
title: architectural masterpiece that radiates grandeur and luxury.

body: This Brazen Palace also known as Bronze Palace Anuradhapura was built 161-137BC by King Dutugemunu It had over a 1000 rooms and was nine stories high. The only remains today are 1600 granite columns arranged in 40 rows. It was known as the Bronze Palace due to the bronze tiled roof it had.. It provided accommodation for up to 1000 monks and attendants. It ws the tallest building up to 993AD
title: Lovamahapaya Brazen Palace

body: There is little so see today of the Brazen Palace. Made of wood, it burnt down several times over the centuries. It may have been a monastic, rather than royal, residence. There are more than a few doubts about the reputed 9 stories, yet alone 1,000 rooms. Some of the pillars presently standing are not original. With some background, a traveler can imagine past grandeur while a tourist will just pass by muttering.
title: AN ODD HISTORICAL STRUCTURE

title: Pillars

body: Nothing much to see here, please move on. Just a cluster of stone pillars each not more than 3 metres tall, without even ornamentation. You will see a roofed building, but it's a recent replica of (what?) modern imagination of what the "palace" might have looked like?It's fenced off; you can't even wander among the stones.This site is located a short walk northwest of the Sri Maha Bodhi Temple, so you may want to take a peek at it while walking from the Temple to the Ruwanvelisaya Dagoba. A one-minute peek is more than it deserves. At least one does not need to pay to get near the site.
title: If gazing at stone stubs is your thing

body: That's why I'm giving this 3 stars. Convenience. (And it's got a cool background story as well). As others have mentioned it's not something you should go out of your way in seeing specifically, - unless the remaining stones of the Brazen Palace offers something you know you're interested in for some reason. However it's very conveniently located if you're visiting the major sites of Anuradhapura. There's a path that runs between the Jethawanaramaya and the Sri Maha Bodhi. As you exit the sacred tree, just continue forward across the street. The pedestrian path that leads north is the Swarnamali Mawatha. To your right will be the Lovamahapaya (Brazen Palace). (And if you continue on down the road for under 10 minutes you will end up at the Ruwanwelisaya). This ruin is locked away behind a metal fence so you wont get close. There is a built up house/structure in the center but it's a replica. Still, I suppose it helps one imagine something, anything here besides the remnants of 1600 columns that once supported 9 stories reaching 150 feet with 1000 rooms. Since you're here, look across the pedestrian path and you might notice the ruins of Ransimalakaya, an open sided meeting hall.
title: Right on the road...

body: The fascination is imagining the nine story building with a bronze roof that once stood here. Nowadays, the remains of 1600 concrete columns on the ground floor are all that remain, and you can only view these through a fence. However, the palace is immediately to the right as you exit the Sri Maha Bodhi, so it is easy to view.
title: 1600 stone columns all that remains of a nine story building accommodating 1000 monks

body: You get to see a 17th century like house surrounded by hundreds of stone pillars that were part of the palace that once was. Worth taking a picture as its conveniently located, nothing more.
title: Quite disappointing

body: Not really much to see here apart from some columns that might or might not have been part of the Brazen Palace. It is across from the Ruwanwelisaya Dagoba.
title: Mostly ruins

body: I have read a number of reviews that have been somewhat disparaging about this 'ruin' which I view as disappointing and perhaps lacking judgement. The Brazen Palace lies between the sacred Bo tree and an enormous dagoba, both of which are must-see things during the tour of the sacred city in Anuradhapura. So you don't have to go out of your way to see it. The sheer number of pillars which would have supported the roof structure after which the palace was named is very impressive and I've not seen anything else with pillars on this scale. As with many buildings here and elsewhere in Asia (eg Cambodia) the stone supporting structures of buildings have stood the test of time better than roof structures which were largely wooden and have either trotted away or been taken for other buildings or firewood. So go and have a look and use your imagination as to what it would have looked like. failing that check out the museum
title: A most unusual building. Worth a look

body: We're sure that the 'Brazen Palace' will have been quite a spectacle in its day - but the reality now - is 1,600 unornate fenced off columns. Worth a quick photo if you're passing it on the way to the sacred bodhi tree but not worth going out of your way (in our opinion).
title: A one minute photographic opportunity

body: Lovamahapaya is otherwise known as Brazen Place because of the bronze tiles that were used on its roof. It is of interest to those fascinated by the architecture and construction techniques of ancient times and adds to the amazing variety of cultural highlights to be found in the Anuradhapura area. Today Lovamahapaya is rather dilapidated but one can appreciate the magnificence of the original building with its 1,600 stone pillars.
title: Interesting architecturally

body: The palace with 1,600 stone pillars in 40 rows sheltered 1,000 windowed chambers in the past has now became a barren site with several broken pillars and shabby structure being fenced off. Next to it you could find a 45- feet rice boat cut from a stone and capable to prepare alms for 3,000 monks at a time in the defunct Mahavihara monastry in the past. You could not expect to find too much from the site during your visit here.
title: History and current situation

body: Sri Lanka has many beautiful ruins. The brazen palace is 90% imagination and 10% granite columns (there are many of these though). When I say 'granite columns', I do not mean the elaborate carved variety. It looks more like a construction site than an ancient ruin.
title: Disappointing

Very near the Bo tree, so you'll probably be doing both at the same time. Take your socks, to protect our soft feet, this is acceptable and respectful in the shrine areas.

body: The fenced off 1600 pillars are all that remains of what was once a palace of great heights. It's impressive to look at them and think that they are more than 2000 years old.
title: Impressive History

body: This too is located in Anuradhapura close to Sri Maha Bodhi and Ruwanwelisaya. This was used as a place to get the Buddhist Monks assembled on “Poya” days to recite the “Pirith”. According to history this was a nine story building done by King “Dutugemunu” who built the “Ruwanwelisya”.
